structure.title: Act I, scene 1 · The map · Giving a kingdom away
structure.text: Lear intends to give his daughters land in proportion to their declarations of love. He also intends to keep the name of king and a substantial following. The ceremony goes wrong before anybody has worked out who will pay for the horses and feed the men.

structure.title: Act I, scene 2 · Two fathers read their children
structure.text: Lear hears Cordelia refuse to compete with her sisters. Gloucester reads a letter about his son Edgar supplied by his other son Edmund. In both households the child who helps a father interpret the evidence has an interest in the interpretation.

structure.title: Act I, scene 3 – Act III · The storm · Who can get indoors?
structure.text: A dispute over how many followers Lear may keep becomes a question of shelter. Outside, an old man accustomed to ordering others to attend him discovers who has long been exposed to weather without an escort or a roof.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · Dover · Meeting people in altered circumstances
structure.text: On the road, people guide strangers, take messages and come upon people they once knew under very different conditions. An act of care may require concealing one's identity. News of armies gathers around these precarious meetings.

people.name: Cordelia, Goneril and Regan
people.text: The older sisters give the eloquent answers their father rewards. Cordelia resists his demand. Later, providing a home for a king who still behaves like a sovereign will be a daily problem quite apart from anybody's speech at the ceremony.

people.name: Edmund and Edgar
people.text: Edgar enjoys the security of a legitimate heir. Edmund has heard his father joke about his birth in company. His resentment of a real injustice gives him a particularly effective means of recruiting sympathy for what he chooses to do.

people.name: Kent and the Fool
people.role: Servants who speak against the king
people.text: Kent risks banishment by contradicting Lear. The Fool can get a little further by disguising criticism as a song or joke. Even he keeps testing how much truth his employer will hear in a single sitting.

context.title: What Lear thinks retirement will buy
context.text: Lear divides the power to govern while reserving the honours and armed company of a ruler. His daughters inherit real responsibilities without a shared understanding of the authority attached to them. Their quarrel can begin over the conduct of one noisy household.

context.title: Disguise moves into the family
context.text: Banishment and accusation make recognisable faces dangerous. The audience can know when a child is attending a parent who sees only a stranger. That imbalance lends an apparently ordinary offer of help extraordinary tenderness.

notice.text: When does Lear ask somebody else whether they are cold?
notice.why: A small question about another body can mark a large change in what the king is able to notice. His most searching political discoveries come once he has lost the power to issue policy.

A kingdom is divided, followers are counted and each side asks how many the king really needs. An apparently practical calculation gets very close to asking what anyone needs in order to live as a human being.

notice.text: Who takes the risk of saying stop?
notice.why: Commands still require attendants willing to carry them out. A comparatively minor figure can reveal the moral cost of an order by objecting to it while there is still time to act.

opening: Lear offers his daughters portions of his kingdom according to how extravagantly they declare their love. He wants to give up the work of ruling while keeping the deference, comfort, and authority. One daughter refuses to perform the speech he expects. The consequences spread from a family ceremony into a country where people must choose between telling the truth and remaining safe. Shakespeare strips an old king of the arrangements that made him feel loved, leaving others to discover what they owe him without the crown.
